mSub: We count the fire that satellites have seen since 2001 and put it on a single scale, so that each year can be compared with normal.
mFoco1: Each satellite passes over the peninsula twice a day, once by day and once by night, and marks the places where it detects the heat of a fire. We divide the map into squares, and a hot spot is a 1 km square with fire on one day: if the same square burns for three days, it counts three times.
mFoco2: The satellite sees any fire: it cannot tell a milpa burn from a wildfire. And no hot spots does not mean there was no fire, because clouds and smoke hide it and a very small fire can slip past.
mUnirTitulo: How we joined 25 years of satellites
mUnir1: Satellites were added over the years, and adding up what all of them see would inflate recent years. So we use one for each period:
mUnir2: Today's satellites (VIIRS) see smaller fires than earlier ones (MODIS). In the season, for every square with fire that Aqua saw in Yucatán, today's satellites see between {a} and {b}, depending on the zone. Using the years they flew together, we calculated a factor for each zone and time of year, and with it we brought the MODIS years to today's scale.
mGrafTitulo: Hot spots in Yucatán, March 1 to May 31 of each year
mRayas: Hatched: MODIS years brought to the VIIRS scale.
mSaltoCrudo: Without calibration, fire seems to have multiplied by {c} from {a1}–{a2} to {d1}–{d2}.
mSaltoArmonizado: Calibrated, it multiplies by {r} (1 = no jump). This is Yucatán in the burning season; below is the test with the whole peninsula and the full year.
mCrudoAria: Without calibration: from 2001 to 2011 the bars stay very low and fire seems to jump in 2012.
mArmonizadoAria: With the calibration: the years from 2001 to 2011 rise and come close to today’s.
mConfiarIntro: We checked the series with four tests. The goal of each one was set before seeing the result.

mSatTitulo: Each satellite against the joined series
mSatIntro: Pick a satellite and compare it with the K'áak' series (Yucatán, March 1 to May 31). Without calibration, the MODIS satellites see much less fire than the VIIRS ones. Calibrated, each satellite should land close to the series.
mSatAria: K'áak' series from {a} to {b} as bars and {s} as a line.
mSatIncompleto: {s} in the season. In {a} it misses the start of the season.
mSatDifIndep: typical difference from the series, in {n} years we used neither in the series nor to compute its factor.
mSatDifMismos: typical difference from the series, from {a} to {b}. Its factor was computed with these same years: this is not an independent check.
mSatReferenciaT: From {a} to {b} the series is {s}, with no factor: both lines are the same.
mSatNota: 1 km squares with fire each day in Yucatán, March 1 to May 31. Each satellite is counted on its own, never added to another.
mSatNotaTerra: Terra is the oldest satellite, and NASA confirms it is drifting from its orbit; in its last years it falls below the series. The series only uses Terra until July 3, 2002.
mSatNotaAqua: Aqua carries the series from 2003 to 2011. In 2022 it spent 17 days without sending data because of a failure NASA reported, and the rest of the season it saw fewer hot spots than S-NPP. We do not know why yet.
mSatNotaSNPP: S-NPP is the reference: from January 20, 2012 to November 2, 2026 the series is S-NPP. The other satellites are calibrated to its scale.
mSatNotaNOAA20: NOAA-20 continues the series from November 3, 2026. Its FIRMS record starts on April 1, 2018, so that year it misses March.

mDescarga1: The complete harmonized series, with every week from 2001 to 2026 in {n} municipalities of the peninsula and the normal for each week. The boundaries we use do not yet include the three newest municipalities (Dzitbalché, Seybaplaya and Puerto Morelos), so their fire counts in the municipality they split from. It is a CSV table that Excel opens; the column names are in the first row.
mPie: Data: FIRMS (NASA), {a} to {b}, and CONAFOR wildfire records, {d} to {h}. Updated {f}.
valSalto2012PasaDentro: Pass: uncalibrated, hot spots multiply by {razonCruda} from {antesDesde}–{antesHasta} to {despuesDesde}–{despuesHasta}. Calibrated, they come to {razonArmonizada} times the earlier level (1 = no jump). That is within normal year-to-year variation ({naturalMin} to {naturalMax}). Years before and after 2012 can be compared.
valSalto2012PasaFuera: Pass: uncalibrated, hot spots multiply by {razonCruda} from {antesDesde}–{antesHasta} to {despuesDesde}–{despuesHasta}. Calibrated, they come to {razonArmonizada} times the earlier level (1 = no jump). That meets the target set in advance (0.67 to 1.50). But it is outside normal year-to-year variation ({naturalMin} to {naturalMax}): part of the jump may still come from the satellite.
valSalto2012NoPasaDentro: Fail: the target was to remove at least half of the jump and land between 0.67 and 1.50. We set it in advance. Calibration removes {reduccionPct}% of the jump and brings hot spots to {razonArmonizada} times the earlier level (1 = no jump). That is within normal year-to-year variation ({naturalMin} to {naturalMax}), but it does not change the verdict. We cannot say calibration fixes the satellite change.
valSalto2012NoPasaFuera: Fail: the target was to remove at least half of the jump and land between 0.67 and 1.50. We set it in advance. Calibration removes {reduccionPct}% of the jump and brings hot spots to {razonArmonizada} times the earlier level (1 = no jump). That is outside normal year-to-year variation ({naturalMin} to {naturalMax}). Years before 2012 cannot be compared with later ones yet.
valSalto2012Limitaciones: We only check the 2012 satellite change, using three-year averages, not each year from 2001 to 2011.
Normal variation comes from comparing S-NPP periods from 2013 to 2025. There are seven, and they overlap: a reference, not a statistical test.
We measure the whole peninsula over the whole year. A municipality or the burning season alone may differ: Yucatán state goes from ×{razonCrudaYucatan} to ×{razonArmonizadaYucatan}.
valAquaFueraMuestraNombre: Aqua in years outside the calibration
valAquaFueraMuestraPasaZonaEpoca: Pass: we tested the calibration on {desde}–{hasta}, years we left out of it. Converted by zone and season, Aqua was off from S-NPP by {wapeZonaEpocaPct}% on average; with a single factor, by {wapeUnicoPct}%. The limit, set in advance, was 25%. Aqua years, 2002 to 2011, may be off by about that much.
valAquaFueraMuestraPasaUnico: Pass with a single factor: we tested the calibration on {desde}–{hasta}, years we left out of it. Converted with one factor, Aqua was off from S-NPP by {wapeUnicoPct}% on average. Splitting by zone and season does not improve it enough ({wapeZonaEpocaPct}%). The limit, set in advance, was 25%. Aqua years, 2002 to 2011, may be off by about that much.
valAquaFueraMuestraNoPasaZonaEpoca: Fail: we tested the calibration on {desde}–{hasta}, years we left out of it. Converted by zone and season, Aqua was off from S-NPP by {wapeZonaEpocaPct}% on average; with a single factor, by {wapeUnicoPct}%. The limit, set in advance, was 25%. Aqua years, 2002 to 2011, may be off by more than we set as acceptable.
valAquaFueraMuestraNoPasaUnico: Fail: we tested the calibration on {desde}–{hasta}, years we left out of it. Converted with one factor, Aqua was off from S-NPP by {wapeUnicoPct}% on average; by zone and season, by {wapeZonaEpocaPct}%. The limit, set in advance, was 25%. Aqua years, 2002 to 2011, may be off by more than we set as acceptable.
valAquaFueraMuestraLimitaciones: We compare against S-NPP, which also misses fires: this shows whether the satellites match, not how much fire there was.
The error pools five years and all zones; the chart shows it year by year. In one municipality or one week it can be larger.

In 2022, Aqua sent no data for 17 days after a failure reported by NASA; we leave those days out. The rest of the season it saw fewer hot spots than usual against S-NPP, while its twin Terra did not. We do not know why yet.
We only test Aqua. Terra, which covers 2001 to mid-2002, has no test like this.
valConaforCumple: Met: of {incendios} wildfires recorded by CONAFOR, {realSnpp}% had S-NPP hot spots nearby; by chance, {azarSnpp}%. Of those over 100 hectares, {grandesSnpp}%. The target, set in advance, was at least three times chance and 75% of the large ones.
valConaforNoCumple: Not met: of {incendios} wildfires recorded by CONAFOR, {realSnpp}% had S-NPP hot spots nearby; by chance, {azarSnpp}%. Of those over 100 hectares, {grandesSnpp}%. The target, set in advance, was at least three times chance and 75% of the large ones.
valConaforLimitaciones: This test is informative: it checks whether the satellite detects fires, not the conversion between satellites.
CONAFOR's records are wildfires from 2015 to 2024, not agricultural burns. This says nothing about burning dates.
We count any hot spot within 2 km, from a day before to a day after the fire. Since there is fire everywhere in the season, we also measure what would match by chance.
Small fires slip past more often: of those of 5 hectares or less, {chicosSnpp}% had hot spots nearby.
valViirsPasaNoaa21Cumple: Pass: from {aniosDesde} to {aniosHasta}, NOAA-20 with its factor counted between {razonMinNoaa20} and {razonMaxNoaa20} for each S-NPP hot spot. The target, set in advance, was 0.90 to 1.10 every year. So the series can continue with NOAA-20 without a jump like 2012's. NOAA-21, in its two full years, also meets the target ({razonMinNoaa21} to {razonMaxNoaa21}).
valViirsPasaNoaa21NoCumple: Pass: from {aniosDesde} to {aniosHasta}, NOAA-20 with its factor counted between {razonMinNoaa20} and {razonMaxNoaa20} for each S-NPP hot spot. The target, set in advance, was 0.90 to 1.10 every year. So the series can continue with NOAA-20 without a jump like 2012's. NOAA-21, in its two full years, misses the target ({razonMinNoaa21} to {razonMaxNoaa21}); it is not part of the series.
valViirsNoPasaNoaa21Cumple: Fail: from {aniosDesde} to {aniosHasta}, NOAA-20 with its factor counted between {razonMinNoaa20} and {razonMaxNoaa20} for each S-NPP hot spot. The target, set in advance, was 0.90 to 1.10 every year and at most 5% total difference. The difference was {diferenciaPctNoaa20}%. Continuing with NOAA-20, the series may have a jump. NOAA-21, in its two full years, does meet the target ({razonMinNoaa21} to {razonMaxNoaa21}).
valViirsNoPasaNoaa21NoCumple: Fail: from {aniosDesde} to {aniosHasta}, NOAA-20 with its factor counted between {razonMinNoaa20} and {razonMaxNoaa20} for each S-NPP hot spot. The target, set in advance, was 0.90 to 1.10 every year and at most 5% total difference. The difference was {diferenciaPctNoaa20}%. Continuing with NOAA-20, the series may have a jump. NOAA-21, in its two full years, does not meet it either ({razonMinNoaa21} to {razonMaxNoaa21}).
valViirsLimitaciones: We calculated NOAA-20's factor from these same years, so the factor pulls the total difference ({diferenciaPctNoaa20}%) toward zero. What tells us something is each year on its own.
We compare VIIRS with VIIRS: this shows whether the series jumps at a switch, not whether they see every fire.
NOAA-21 has been in FIRMS since March 2023, so it overlaps S-NPP for only two full years. It has no factor and is not part of the series.
mIA: We built this project with the help of artificial intelligence (Claude, by Anthropic) for research, code and drafting. The team chose the method and checked every figure against its source.
